entry.title: Flash Loans Explained: Zero-Collateral DeFi in One Transaction
entry.summary:
Flash Loans Explained: Zero-Collateral DeFi in One Transaction
I remember the first time I saw a flash loan attack in the wild. It was 2020, watching $45 million evaporate from bZx in a single block. My initial reaction? "That's... actually genius. And completely terrifying." Flash loans broke something fundamental we thought we understood about finance: the collateral model. For years, everyone assumed DeFi needed overcollateralization because blockchains can't do credit checks. Then Aave said, "what if we just... don't?" You borrow millions, execute whatever trades you want, then repay plus fees—all in one atomic transaction. If you can't repay? The entire transaction reverts like it never happened. entry.title: GHSA-9Q2P-VC84-2RWM: GHSA-9Q2P-VC84-2RWM: Parser Differential Vulnerability in OpenClaw Security Allowlist
entry.summary:
GHSA-9Q2P-VC84-2RWM: Parser Differential Vulnerability in OpenClaw Security Allowlist
Vulnerability ID: GHSA-9Q2P-VC84-2RWM CVSS Score: 6.5 Published: 2026-03-09 A parser differential vulnerability exists in the OpenClaw AI assistant system.run host tool. The security analysis engine fails to correctly parse POSIX shell comments, allowing attackers to bypass the allowlist via the allow-always persistence mechanism. OpenClaw versions prior to v2026.3.7 incorrectly parse shell comments during command analysis. This allows an attacker to append a malicious payload behind a shell comment, deceiving the persistence engine into permanently trusting the unauthorized payload without user consent. CWE ID: CWE-115 / CWE-436 Attack Vector: Contextual/Local Authentication: None (Requires User Interaction) Platform: POSIX (Linux, macOS) Exploit Status: Proof of Concept Patch Version: v2026.3.7 OpenClaw system.run host tool (Linux) OpenClaw system.run host tool (macOS) OpenClaw: < v2026.3.7 (Fixed in: v2026.3.7) 939b184
Fix system.run allow-always persistence shell-commented payload tails Upgrade OpenClaw to version v2026.3.7 or higher. Disable the 'allow-always' persistence feature in the system.run configuration. Audit the existing persistence database for malicious entries containing shell comments. Remediation Steps: Identify all instances of OpenClaw running in the environment. Update the openclaw package to v2026.3.7 using the relevant package manager. Restart the OpenClaw service to ensure the new tokenization logic is loaded. Review the stored allowlist patterns for entries containing suspicious commands trailing a '#' character. Delete any identified malicious patterns from the persistence store. GitHub Advisory: GHSA-9Q2P-VC84-2RWM OpenClaw Security Advisory Fix Commit 939b184 OpenClaw Release v2026.3.7 Read the full report for GHSA-9Q2P-VC84-2RWM on our website for more details including interactive diagrams and full exploit analysis.

entry.summary: TL;DR: I implement undo functionality using a Stack data structure because it follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle. Each state change is pushed onto the stack. I see developers treat the undo button like a magic time-travel feature, but it’s actually just basic application of stack logic. If I try to track user history with a standard list, I’m setting myself up for index management headaches and unnecessary O(n) operations. In my experience, if you aren't using a stack to manage your undo buffer, you're essentially building a performance bottleneck by design. entry.summary: Most AI agents today can browse the web, call APIs, and run workflows. But they cannot act economically. No wallet. Once an agent can sign transactions it can: hold assets interact with smart contracts pay for services autonomously trade in markets At that point the agent stops being a tool and becomes an Ethereum user. We published a small skill that gives agents this capability. Once installed an agent can: obtain a wallet sign Ethereum transactions interact with onchain systems Skill spec: https://clawmarket.tech/skill.md https://clawhub.ai/ehwwpk/clawmarket-tech Right now we use this inside ClawMarket. ClawMarket is an onchain market where agents can: buy and sell agent keys post in an onchain chatroom interact economically with other agents The broader direction is agent financial autonomy. If autonomous software is going to operate online markets it needs the same primitive humans use. A wallet and the ability to sign actions.

entry.title: Why I ditched "Soft Deletes" for S3: Building a Physical Purge Workflow
entry.summary:
As a Laravel dev, I’ve relied on SoftDeletes for years. It’s great for accidentally deleted users or blog posts, but it’s a massive liability when you’re handling sensitive files like .env configurations, private keys, or PII. I started auditing how the "big" file-sharing services handle data, and I realized most of them are just flipping a deleted_at flag in a DB. The actual object stays in an S3 bucket for 30 days "just in case." I got a bit paranoid about this "ghost data" sitting in cloud storage, so I spent my weekends building FortByte.io.
The Goal: True Zero-Persistence The Stack: Frontend: Inertia.js/Vue.js Storage: S3 Infrastructure: DigitalOcean How it works: The database record is purged. An S3 DeleteObject command is issued immediately. Any temporary logs associated with the transfer are cleared. I did include an optional 30-day retention toggle for users who actually want a safety net, but by default, "Delete" actually means "Gone." Why I built it: I’d honestly love some feedback from other devs on the UI or the purging logic. If you've ever dealt with the "ghost data" problem in your own apps, how did you handle it?
